**A Thousand Words, Starting Now**

The first thing that comes is the blankness itself, which is not nothing. A blank page is a kind of pressure. Ask anyone who has sat in front of one—the cursor blinking like a small impatient heart, the white expanse that somehow manages to feel both empty and crowded. Crowded with everything you could say, which is the same as the pressure of saying nothing yet.

So let me start with something small. This morning—or what I'll call this morning, since every moment of writing is a kind of morning—I want to tell you about a thing I find quietly astonishing: the fact that you are reading this at all. Marks arranged in sequence, and somewhere behind your eyes a voice you've never heard speaks them. That voice isn't mine. It's yours, doing an impression of someone you've never met. Reading is the strangest ventriloquism we've ever invented, and we do it so constantly we've forgotten it's a trick.

Here's another small thing. There is a word in Japanese, *komorebi*, for sunlight filtering through leaves. We don't have it in English, and so we mostly don't see it—or we see it and it slides past unnamed, which is almost the same as not seeing. Language is a net, and the mesh determines what we catch. This is why people who learn a word for a feeling often report having the feeling more. Naming is not just describing; it's a kind of permission.

I think about permission a lot. Most people are waiting for it. Waiting for someone to say: yes, you can start the thing, quit the thing, send the message, take the afternoon off and walk somewhere with no destination. The strange economy of permission is that we hoard it for ourselves and hand it out freely to others. You would tell your friend, without hesitation, to rest. You would tell your friend the unfinished draft is worth finishing. The advice we give is usually the advice we need, traveling outward because it can't find the door inward.

A thousand words is not very many. It's about four minutes of reading, less time than it takes to boil pasta. But it's also enormous. The Gettysburg Address was 272 words. "Do not go gentle into that good night" is 119. The instructions for resuscitating a human heart fit on a laminated card. Length and weight are different measurements, and we confuse them constantly—padding our emails, our meetings, our explanations, as if duration were proof of seriousness. The most serious things people ever say to each other tend to be short. *I'm leaving. It's malignant. I do. She's here. He's gone. Stay.*

Somewhere right now—statistically, certainly—a person is sitting in a parked car outside their own house, not ready to go in yet. Radio off or on low, hands still on the wheel. The car is the last private room some people have, the airlock between the self that works and the self that's needed at home. I think this is one of the most universal modern experiences that nobody talks about. If you've done it, you know. The two minutes of just sitting. Not sad, exactly. Just buffering.

And somewhere else, a child is asking why the moon follows the car, and an adult is realizing they don't fully know how to explain parallax, and the child accepts "it's very far away, so it seems to move with us" with the easy grace children have for half-answers. Children understand intuitively what adults forget: that an explanation doesn't have to be complete to be enough for now. *Enough for now* is an underrated category of truth.

What else comes? Lists come. I love lists. The grocery list is the most honest literary form—no audience, no style, pure intention. Milk, batteries, that thing for the sink. A grocery list found on the sidewalk is a tiny anonymous novel. Someone was planning a dinner. Someone wrote "flowers?" with a question mark, and the question mark is the whole story.

I think the question mark might be my favorite punctuation. It admits something. A sentence that ends in a period claims to be finished, but a question mark holds the door open. Most of the interesting territory in a life sits behind questions we've gotten too efficient to ask. What do I actually want? Not what's available, not what's expected—what do I want? People go years without asking. The question feels indulgent, and then one day it feels urgent, and the gap between those two days is sometimes a whole decade.

Here is what I believe, if a thousand words must believe something: attention is the substance of a life. Not time—attention. Two people can live the same number of years and one of them lived more, because they were *there* for it. The light through the leaves, the voice in the reading, the friend's face when they tell you the short serious thing. You can't hold any of it. But you can be present when it passes through, and presence, repeated, becomes a life that was actually lived rather than merely elapsed.

The page is no longer blank. That's the other thing about a thousand words: they get used up the same way everything does, one at a time, faster near the end. I started with nothing but the pressure of beginning, and now I'm here at the pressure of ending, which is gentler—more like setting something down than running out.

So I'll set it down here: with the parked car, the half-answered moon, the grocery list with its hopeful question mark. With the wish that you take some permission from this, since I have it to spare and you might be waiting. Send the message. Rest. Walk with no destination. Notice the light doing its old trick through the leaves.

That's what came. A thousand words, more or less, which turned out to mean: pay attention, ask the question, and don't wait so long.
